conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’ll be guiding you through a quick check-in today. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, and it helps us figure out the best support for you.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our care team. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you over the past seven days. We’ll go through 10 questions; each one is straightforward, and we’ll take it at your pace. If anything feels uncomfortable, we can pause at any time.

Ready to begin? 

First, I’d love to know: over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things you used to enjoy, or has that felt harder lately?

[soft smile, eyes a little tired]  
It’s… harder. I mean, I still get a tiny spark when I think about grabbing coffee with my best friend or flipping through my favorite cooking magazine, but by the time I have a free second I’m so drained that it feels pointless. Things that used to excite me—like planning little weekend outings—just feel flat, like the color’s been sucked out of them.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, eyes on the floor]  
Not really… I’ll catch myself half-smiling if the baby makes a silly face or if my husband cracks a joke, but it fades fast. Most of the time I feel too heavy to really laugh—like the sound won’t quite come out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quietly]  
Not much… I try to tell myself I’ll enjoy a walk or a hot shower once the baby sleeps, but when the moment comes it feels kind of gray. I still plan little things—like watching a show I used to love—but when I actually do them the excitement’s just not there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes flick down to my lap, voice small]  
Yeah… like if the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. Last night he cried for twenty minutes and I kept replaying the whole day, sure I’d messed up somehow. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but the guilt still swoops in every time.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, twisting the edge of my sleeve]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet—so I’ll check his breathing three times in five minutes. Or I’ll lie in bed after he’s finally asleep and my mind just spins: what if the crib rail isn’t locked, what if the monitor dies, what if I miss something and he gets hurt. None of it has actually happened, but the worry feels stuck on repeat.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes… it’s like a sudden wave. Yesterday I was folding his tiny onesies and out of nowhere my chest got tight, heart pounding, and I had to sit down because I was sure something awful was about to happen. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky. It keeps coming back—those flashes of fear—even when everything looks fine on the outside.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]  
Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks. I’ll start one thing—put the baby down, wash a bottle, swap the laundry—and before I finish, he’s crying again and I’m right back at square one. By dinner I’m snapping at my husband over nothing, then crying because I feel so overwhelmed. I keep thinking, “I’m supposed to be handling this better,” but the pile never shrinks and neither does the pressure in my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet voice, rubbing my thumb against my other palm]  
Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling every little thing I might’ve done wrong or forgotten. It takes me forever to drift off, and then I jolt awake sure I heard the baby—even when the monitor’s quiet. Some nights I’m awake two or three times, heart racing, and I can’t settle back down. By morning I’m more tired than when I went to bed.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes well up a little]  
Most of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. I’ll look at the baby sleeping and feel love, but right behind it is this ache. Little things—seeing a diaper commercial, hearing a song on the radio—can make my throat tight. The sadness isn’t every single minute, but it keeps rolling back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, eyes fixed on hands]  
A couple of times this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and just burst into tears—couldn’t stop. It’s not dramatic sobbing, more like this quiet leak I can’t turn off when everything feels too much.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[swallows hard, barely above a whisper]  
Once or twice… I’ll be staring at the bottles in the sink and this quick image pops in—what if I just kept my head under the bathwater, or what if I walked out and didn’t come back. It’s never a real plan, just this flash that scares me, gone as fast as it came. I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thought still surfaces when everything feels hopeless.

You've shared how hard each day has felt since your baby arrived-how joy seems dulled, laughter slips away, and even simple tasks feel overwhelming. You described constant worry, sudden surges of fear, nights spent wide-awake with racing thoughts, and a lingering sadness that settles over everything. You also mentioned brief, scary thoughts of escape that you don't want to act on but that still frighten you. Your honesty shows strength, and these feelings are not your fault; many new mothers struggle in silence, and help is available.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes near-absence of laughter, only fleeting half-smiles that fade fast, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>She still makes plans but reports the actual enjoyment is "just not there," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, pervasive self-blame for normal infant behavior, indicating this occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries occurring "pretty much every day" with physical symptoms (racing heart) and repetitive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, recurrent panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) occurring without clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to complete basic tasks, emotional dysregulation, and persistent chest pressure—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the time" with persistent ache and emotional triggers, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive self-harm images occurring "once or twice" that align with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 25 exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. Patient endorses <sym>depressed mood most days</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>initial and middle insomnia</sym>, <sym>diminished ability to concentrate</sym>, and <sym>recurrent passive suicidal ideation</sym> without intent. These symptoms cause clinically significant distress and impairment in caring for her infant. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Request immediate safety plan including 24/7 support person, removal of potential hazards, and emergency contacts
3. Offer referral to <med>mother-baby psychiatric inpatient or day-program</med> if available
4. Provide telephone follow-up within 24-48 hours to review mood, safety, and medication options
5. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> specializing in postpartum mood
6. Discuss <med>sertraline</med> or compatible <med>SSRI</med> if breastfeeding; benefits usually outweigh risks
7. Encourage 20-minute daytime walk, balanced meals, and acceptance of household help to reduce overload
8. Connect with local <med>postpartum support group</med> or online communities for peer encouragement
9. Give clear emergency instructions: call 911 or national suicide prevention lifeline if thoughts escalate
10. Schedule re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Surveillance  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed across 10-item EPDS-style interview  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-if” worries, nocturnal hyper-arousal  
- Sudden panic-like surges (chest tightness, fear of imminent harm)  
- Overwhelm with routine tasks, sense of “drowning,” irritability  
- Initial insomnia and middle-of-night anxious awakenings  
- Passive self-harm ideation (brief images of drowning, leaving); denies intent or plan  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with functioning and bonding, worse at night.  
Risk factors: Primiparous status, sleep deprivation, perfectionistic self-expectations.  
Safety: Endorses fleeting passive suicidal thoughts; no disclosed intent, plan, or preparatory behavior.  

Screening impression: High clinical concern for major depressive episode with anxious features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder.  
Recommendation: Complete standardized EPDS score; urgent safety plan; referral for immediate perinatal mental-health evaluation and follow-up support.
